lead: A transmission line is a distributed circuit: every metre adds series resistance and inductance and shunt conductance and capacitance, the four primary constants. Put them into the telegrapher's equations and the solution is two waves travelling in opposite directions, with one characteristic impedance Z0 and one propagation constant γ. From γ come attenuation, phase constant, wavelength and velocity. Every RF design, from a 50 Ω cable to a printed trace, starts here.
prereq: You need: Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws, phasor notation with angular frequency ω = 2πf, complex numbers in rectangular and polar form, and the physical idea that a wire stores magnetic energy while two nearby conductors store electric energy.

blocks.text: A transmission line always has a go and a return conductor: the inner and outer of a coaxial cable, a microstrip trace over a ground plane, or a twisted pair.

At radio and microwave frequency the line is long compared with the wavelength, so voltage and current change from centimetre to centimetre. We therefore describe a short slice of length Δz and let Δz shrink to zero.
Some syllabi call R, L, G and C the primary line constants. All four are per metre: a 20 m cable has total series inductance 20L, not L.

sections.h3: Telegrapher's equations and the general solution

blocks.text: Take a slice Δz, apply Kirchhoff's voltage law round the series path and Kirchhoff's current law at the shunt node, divide by Δz and let Δz → 0. In phasor form:
dV/dz = −(R + jωL) I        dI/dz = −(G + jωC) V
blocks.where: V and I are phasor voltage and current at distance z from the sending end, in V and A; R, L, G, C are per-metre constants; ω = 2πf rad/s; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: Differentiate the first equation and substitute the second. The voltage obeys d²V/dz² = γ²V, with

blocks.where: γ is the propagation constant; α is the attenuation constant in nepers per metre (Np/m); β is the phase constant in radians per metre (rad/m).
V⁺ is the forward wave amplitude at z = 0, V⁻ is the backward wave amplitude, both in V.

blocks.text: The current that goes with it is I(z) = (V⁺/Z0)e<sup>−γz</sup> − (V⁻/Z0)e<sup>γz</sup>, with

blocks.where: Z0 is the characteristic impedance in ohms; it is the ratio V⁺/I⁺ of a single forward wave.

blocks.text: Most real lines are low-loss: R ≪ ωL and G ≪ ωC. Then Z0 ≈ √(L/C), β ≈ ω√(LC) and α ≈ R/(2Z0) + GZ0/2 Np/m. The first term is conductor loss and the second is dielectric loss. One neper is 8.686 dB, so α in dB/m is 8.686α.

The minus sign on the backward current is the step most often lost in exams: the backward wave carries its current the other way. γ and Z0 are called secondary constants because they follow from R, L, G, C rather than being measured separately.
Set R = G = 0. Then the constants become simple:
Z0 = √(L/C)    β = ω√(LC)    vp = 1/√(LC)    λ = 2π/β = vp/f
blocks.where: Z0 in Ω is now purely real; β in rad/m; vp is the phase velocity in m/s; λ in m; f in Hz.

blocks.text: With R and G present, Z0 is complex and α > 0. A pulse contains many frequencies; if α and β/ω change with frequency, the components are attenuated unequally and travel at different speeds, so the pulse arrives smeared. The line is distortionless when R/L = G/C. Then Z0 = √(L/C) is real, β = ω√(LC), and α = √(RG) is flat in frequency. Telephone cables have R/L far above G/C, so loading coils add series inductance to raise L.
An infinite line has no backward wave, so its input impedance is exactly Z0. A finite line ended in Z0 behaves the same; any other load creates the reflected wave of 1.2.

An infinite line has no backward wave, so its input impedance is exactly Z0. A finite line ended in Z0 behaves the same; any other load creates a reflected wave, which is the subject of 1.2, and the impedance seen at the input is covered in 1.3.

In this book every phasor amplitude is a peak value, so the forward-wave power is P⁺ = |V⁺|²/(2Z0) W for real Z0 (with an rms value it would be |V⁺|²/Z0). On a matched line of length l the voltage falls by e<sup>−αl</sup>, so the power that arrives is a fraction e<sup>−2αl</sup> of the power sent: the transmission efficiency of a matched line is η = e<sup>−2αl</sup>.

examples.question: A lossless coaxial line has L = 0.25 μH/m and C = 100 pF/m. (a) Find Z0. (b) Find the phase velocity. (c) Find the wavelength at 100 MHz. (d) How long does a signal take to travel 3 m of this line?
steps: Convert to SI: L = 0.25 μH/m = 2.5×10⁻⁷ H/m; C = 100 pF/m = 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ F/m.
(c) λ = vp/f = 2×10⁸ / 1×10⁸ = 2 m. Check: β = 2π/λ = π rad/m, and ω = 2π×10⁸ rad/s, so ω/β = 2×10⁸ m/s.
examples.answer: Z0 = 50 Ω, vp = 2×10⁸ m/s, λ = 2 m at 100 MHz, and a 3 m delay of 15 ns.

L = 0.25e-6
C = 100e-12
Z0 = (L / C) ** 0.5
vp = 1 / (L * C) ** 0.5
f = 100e6
lam = vp / f
d = 3.0
t = d / vp
print(Z0)

examples.question: A coaxial line has R = 0.1 Ω/m, L = 0.25 µH/m, G = 10 µS/m and C = 100 pF/m. At 10 MHz find (a) Z0, (b) α and β, (c) the loss of 100 m in dB, (d) the L that would make the line distortionless.
steps: Low-loss check: α ≈ R/(2Z0) + GZ0/2 = 0.1/100 + (10⁻⁵ × 50)/2 = 0.00100 + 0.00025 = 0.00125 Np/m. Conductor loss is four-fifths of it.
(c) 8.686 × 0.00125 = 0.01086 dB/m, so 100 m loses 1.09 dB (matched-line efficiency e<sup>−0.25</sup> = 0.779).
(d) R/L = 4×10⁵ s⁻¹ but G/C = 1×10⁵ s⁻¹, so the line distorts. R/L = G/C needs L = RC/G = (0.1 × 10⁻¹⁰)/10⁻⁵ = 1.0 µH/m; then α = √(RG) = 0.0010 Np/m and Z0 = √(L/C) = 100 Ω.
examples.answer: Z0 = 50.0∠−0.14° Ω; α = 0.00125 Np/m, β = 0.3142 rad/m; 1.09 dB per 100 m; L = 1.0 µH/m makes it distortionless.

traps: Per metre versus total: putting the total L of a 20 m cable into √(L/C) gives an answer wrong by √20. Convert to per-metre values first.
Using free-space c for vp. On a line vp = 1/√(LC) is fixed by the dielectric and is normally below c.
Writing Z0 = √(L/C) when R and G are not zero. That formula is the lossless line only; the general Z0 is complex.

Dropping the minus sign in the backward current, I(z) = (V⁺/Z0)e<sup>−γz</sup> − (V⁻/Z0)e<sup>γz</sup>. With a plus sign the backward wave would carry its current the wrong way, and every Γ and Zin built on it comes out wrong.
Thinking Z0 can be measured with an ohmmeter on an open cable. The meter reads the DC open-circuit resistance, which is nearly infinite, not Z0.

quiz.q: Name the four primary line constants, with units, and say where each comes from.
quiz.a: R (Ω/m) from metal resistance, L (H/m) from the magnetic field, G (S/m) from dielectric leakage, C (F/m) from the electric field between conductors.

quiz.q: Why is Z0 real for a lossless line but complex when R and G are present?
quiz.a: Z0 = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)). With R = G = 0 the jω factors cancel, leaving the real number √(L/C), so V and I of one wave are in phase. With R and G present the ratio has an angle, so Z0 is complex (50.0∠−0.14° Ω for the line of worked example 2).

quiz.q: A lossless line has L = 400 nH/m and C = 100 pF/m. Find Z0 and vp.
A line has α = 0.02 Np/m and is 50 m long. Find the transmission efficiency and the loss in dB.
A cable has R/L greater than G/C. Are the high-frequency components of a pulse attenuated more or less than the low ones, and how do loading coils help?
quiz.a: α is not flat: it rises from √(RG) at low frequency towards R/(2Z0) + GZ0/2 at high frequency, and β/ω is not constant, so the high-frequency parts of a pulse are attenuated more and arrive at a different time; the edges round off. This happens whenever R/L ≠ G/C. Loading coils raise L, bringing R/L down to G/C, so α and vp stop depending on frequency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every high-speed link, from a USB cable to the trace between a SerDes chip and a connector, is designed with these same equations; the loss per metre plotted against frequency is the insertion-loss curve on a datasheet. Channel simulators make R rise with frequency (skin effect) and G rise with frequency (dielectric loss), then predict eye diagrams. Search 'telegrapher's equations', 'insertion loss dB per inch' and 'eye diagram'.
